chapter_theme: Three shrine verses, two for Idaimarudur and one for Kazhukkundram, that strip renunciation of its outward marks: forest, air-eating, rags and the begging bowl are nothing without inner love, and the true lover reaches the bliss of knowledge even living with women at home. When wealth goes, mother, wife, child and kin all turn enemy, so the Lord's feet alone are freedom; and wherever this lone body falls, forest or porch, those feet are the life's companion.
structure_note: 311 and 312 belong to the Idaimarudur set (the work's own 2.1 and 2.2); 313 is an unnumbered Kazhukkundram verse placed after them. 313 is built as a string of alternatives (காடோ செடியோ ...) answered by one line, a pattern Pattinathar uses again at 328.

311.reading: What if one takes to the forest, eats the wind, wears rags and carries the bowl? Those without inner love gain nothing. The true lovers of the Lord of Idaimarudur, even staying in the house beside their women, reach the bliss of the home of true knowledge, which is the land of the high gods.
311.nuance: The verse is the poet's own warning against the life he leads in the பொது verses (329 onward): rags, bowl and porch are only outward. வீடு is played on: the lovers stay in the house (வீடே இருப்பினும்) and reach the house of knowledge (ஞான வீடு), release. The line does not say the householder's way is better, only that love decides.

312.reading: Mother is an enemy, the wife one took a great enemy, one's own child an enemy, kin enemies, this whole world an enemy, when, on looking, rare wealth has gone. So, heart that steeps in this love, the golden feet of the Lord of Marudur are freedom.
312.nuance: The condition is in line 3: all these turn enemy when wealth leaves, so the verse is about kin as bought by wealth, not about kin as such. சுதந்திரம், freedom or independence, is the word chosen for the feet, against a family that has become a dependency. The marked question (நீங்கில்!) reads as a condition despite the punctuation.

313.reading: Forest or bush, the seashore, a heavy-laden land, a city or the heart of a city, a fine house or an outer porch: wherever this lone body falls, Lord of lofty Kazhukkundram, your feet are the companion of my life.
313.nuance: The list of places runs from wild to domestic, so the poet does not know and does not choose where he will die; the contrast is between the body that falls somewhere and the உயிர் whose companion is fixed. The outer porch (புறத்திண்ணை) is where the பொது verses say he sleeps.

links.note: Both deny that the outward signs of the ascetic matter: the Kural says neither shaving nor long hair is needed if one quits what the world condemns, and Pattinathar says forest, air, rags and bowl are nothing without inner love. The Kural's test is conduct, Pattinathar's is love, but both move the mark inward.

311 says the true lovers reach release even living in the house with women; 347 describes those free of attachment from the outside: they bathe when they sweat, eat when hungry, sleep, and look like worldly people. Together they say that the renouncer and the householder cannot be told apart by what they do.

Both make standing among people a function of money: the Naladiyar says a man with a few coins gains rank whatever he wears, while one with nothing is lower than a corpse though well born; Pattinathar says mother, wife, child and kin all become enemies once wealth is gone. The Naladiyar counsels on wealth, Pattinathar draws the conclusion that only the Lord's feet are free of the dependence.

Both make the fate of the body after the life leaves a matter of indifference: the Naladiyar asks what it matters whether the corpse is dragged with a rope, buried with care or thrown anywhere; Pattinathar lists forest, shore, city, house and porch as the places where the body may fall and gives the life a companion that does not depend on which.

source_issues: Unit 313 (own id siddhar:thiruppadal-thirattu:u2, திருக்கழுக்குன்றம்) is unnumbered in the source and is grouped by the tool with the two Idaimarudur verses.
